name: Find the plausible-but-wrong
note: AI code is fluent by construction — clean, idiomatic, well-commented — whether or not it's right. Read against your spec, not for style. Pick the real issue, not the red herring.

items.prompt: The AI's dedup function is clean and passes the sample. Reading against your spec (fuzzy match on name + email), you see it builds a set() of exact tuples. The issue?
candidates: It implements exact-match dedup, not the fuzzy match your spec requires — fluent, idiomatic, and solving the wrong problem you'd already clarified against
set() is slower than a list here and should be replaced
The function is missing a docstring
Nothing — it passes the sample input cleanly
items.correct: It implements exact-match dedup, not the fuzzy match your spec requires — fluent, idiomatic, and solving the wrong problem you'd already clarified against
items.explanation: The code is clean and wrong-by-spec. Reading against your preregistered definition of 'duplicate' catches what a style-skim sails past, because the polish actively suppresses skepticism.
items.principle: Read against the spec you committed, not against whether the code looks nice.

items.prompt: An AI-written average(nums) is clean and correct on every example. What do you check first?
candidates: The empty-input case — average([]) divides by zero; clean code on the happy path tells you nothing about the boundary, which is exactly where AI output skips
Whether it uses sum() or a manual loop — a style preference
Whether the parameter is called nums or numbers
Nothing — averaging is too simple to contain a bug
items.correct: The empty-input case — average([]) divides by zero; clean code on the happy path tells you nothing about the boundary, which is exactly where AI output skips
items.explanation: Boundaries are the comprehension priority. Happy-path fluency is no evidence about the empty, the huge, or the malformed input — go there first when you read AI output.
items.principle: When you read AI code, go to the boundary first — that's where fluency hides the gap.

items.prompt: An AI function carries the comment 'safely handles concurrent access', but the code uses a plain dict with no lock. The right read?
candidates: Trust the code, not the comment — the AI generated a plausible-sounding claim the implementation doesn't back; the mismatch is a bug and a cue to scrutinize the rest
Trust the comment; the AI wrote it, so it must have ensured thread safety
Delete the comment and move on
items.correct: Trust the code, not the comment — the AI generated a plausible-sounding claim the implementation doesn't back; the mismatch is a bug and a cue to scrutinize the rest
items.explanation: An AI comment is generated text, not a guarantee. A comment asserting a property the code lacks is a classic plausible-but-wrong tell — and a sign the surrounding code deserves a harder read.
items.principle: An AI comment is a claim, not a guarantee — verify it against the code.
